# Anthropic Debut; New I Bonds Pay 5.51%; Intuit, Ross Stores and Gap After-Hours Earnings

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at \$83 a share on Wednesday, above the range it had marketed, according to CNBC, Bloomberg and Reuters. The reports landed after a split session on Wall Street: the S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight day while the Nasdaq Composite rose, and Federal Reserve officials talked openly about a larger interest rate increase.

#### MARKET SNAPSHOT

- **S&P 500** 7,323.63, down 0.2%
- **Nasdaq Composite** 24,429.88, up 0.4%
- **Dow** 50,198.17, down 1.1%
- **Russell 2000** 2,714.31, up 0.5%
- **10-year Treasury yield** 5.07%, from 5.10% on Tuesday
- **WTI crude** \$83.26, down 3.2%
- **Brent crude** \$91.95, down 1.3%
- **Gold** \$3,722.80, down 3.3%
- **Bitcoin** about \$62,300, down about 3%

*Closing levels for Wednesday, Nov 18, 2026. Oil is front-month futures. Gold is the spot price and Bitcoin the market price shortly before 5 p.m. ET.*

## Anthropic’s IPO priced at \$83, above its range

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, had marketed its shares at **\$70 to \$78**. On Wednesday afternoon CNBC, Bloomberg and Reuters each reported, citing people familiar with the deal, that the company settled on **\$83**. Anthropic had not announced the price itself as of early Wednesday evening.

The company’s latest filing listed **825 million shares** for sale. At \$83 that would raise about \$68.5 billion, by CNBC’s arithmetic. Bloomberg reported that the offering was also enlarged, so the final share count and the total raised are not confirmed. For scale, CNBC put SpaceX’s IPO in June at \$75 billion before extra shares were added.

Demand ran well ahead of supply. Orders came to nearly seven times the shares on offer, according to earlier reports, and up to 20% of the deal was set aside for individual investors through brokerages. An order is a request, and many investors receive fewer shares than they ask for, or none.

The stock is expected to start trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker **ANT**. Large IPOs usually open later in the morning, not at the 9:30 a.m. ET bell, and no time has been set.

> **Why it matters:** Anyone who owns AI stocks, including through index funds heavy in Nvidia, Amazon and Alphabet, gets a direct reading on Thursday of what public investors will pay for one of the companies at the center of the AI build-out. The IPO price is what large investors paid before trading began, and first-day prices in big offerings can swing sharply in either direction.

#### RATES

## Fed minutes show nearly every official expects to raise rates again

The Federal Reserve released the minutes of its Oct 27 to 28 meeting on Wednesday afternoon. Officials voted 10 to 2 at that meeting to hold the benchmark rate at **3.75% to 4.00%**, and the two dissenters wanted an increase. The minutes say "almost all participants" judged that further increases would likely be appropriate, and that "a couple" thought a move larger than a quarter point "could warrant consideration."

Hours earlier, Fed Governor Christopher Waller made the case for a bigger step in a CNBC interview.

> FED'S WALLER SAYS THE FED MAY NEED TO "SHOCK" PEOPLE\
> \
> Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he is very concerned that inflation is heading in the wrong direction and broadening, in a CNBC interview today.\
> \
> He said roughly 70% of the items in the core services basket are rising… [pic.twitter.com/VArE6RJBPb](https://t.co/VArE6RJBPb)
>
> — WOLF (@WOLF_Financial) [November 18, 2026](https://x.com/WOLF_Financial/status/2123037566492447186?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

The minutes also tie inflation to the AI boom. Fed staff called AI-related demand "a material source of inflation risk," according to CNBC’s account of the document. The next meeting is Dec 8 to 9. The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against other major currencies, reached a 19-month high.

> **Why it matters:** Borrowers feel a higher Fed rate first, through credit cards, car loans and adjustable-rate debt, while savers see it in higher yields on cash. Mortgage rates are already climbing: the average 30-year rate rose to 7.35% last week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.
>
> **Nvidia**
>
> ## Nvidia’s board says it will not bring Jensen Huang back, and the stock falls
>
> Nvidia shares opened higher on Wednesday after Tuesday night’s earnings beat, then reversed and closed at **\$150.96**, down 2.9%. It was the stock’s fifth straight decline. Other chipmakers rose, with AMD up 5.3% and Broadcom up 3.7%, which points to a company-specific worry.
>
> That worry is leadership. On the earnings call, Chair Harvey Jones answered the question that had been open since Huang said he would be honored to return.
>
> > Nvidia’s [\$NVDA](https://x.com/search?q=%24NVDA&src=ctag&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) chairman of the board of directors just said this:\
> > \
> > "Jensen Huang, voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO" <https://t.co/qLL8BWzU8x>
> >
> > — Evan (@StockMKTNewz) [November 17, 2026](https://x.com/StockMKTNewz/status/2122813605431443499?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
>
> Jones said the board has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles, will consider candidates from inside and outside the company, and will not rush the choice. He gave no timeline. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, the interim CEO, called it "business as usual" and closed the call with "We’ve got this." Management raised its outlook for revenue growth in its next fiscal year to about 75%, from 70%, CNBC reported.
>
> **Why it matters:** Nvidia is one of the heaviest weights in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, so index fund holders own it whether they picked it or not. Sales are still growing fast, and shareholders now face a CEO search with no end date at the company whose chips the AI industry depends on.
>
> MARKETS
>
> ## Health insurers sink the Dow while retailers rally
>
> The S&P 500’s fifth straight loss is its longest losing streak since June. The Dow fell **561 points**, and one stock did much of the damage: UnitedHealth dropped 10.2%. Humana fell 13.0%.
>
> Insurers sold off over a proposal from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to expand audits of Medicare Advantage plans, the private versions of Medicare, and to reclaim overpayments. The agency estimates about \$90 billion in savings over 10 years, according to press reports. The proposal is open for public comment and could change.
>
> Retailers went the other way after three earnings reports before the open:
>
> **Lowe’s** rose 1.0%. Its adjusted profit of \$3.10 a share included 34 cents from tariff refunds.
>
> **TJX**, the owner of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls, rose 8.0%. Sales at stores open at least a year grew 4%.
>
> **Target** rose 4.0% and raised its sales forecast for the year.

> TARGET [\$TGT](https://x.com/search?q=%24TGT&src=ctag&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) JUST REPORTED Q3 EARNINGS\
> \
> – Revenue: \$27.07B, beating expectations of \$26.55B 🟢\
> – Adj EPS: \$2.65, beating expectations of \$2.07 🟢 (incl. tariff refund)\
> – Comparable Sales: +5.6%\
> – Gross Margin: 30.5% (w/ tariff refund)\
> \
> Raises FY26 Guidance:\
> – Adj EPS:… [pic.twitter.com/1kpjYsGrwR](https://t.co/1kpjYsGrwR)
>
> — WOLF (@WOLF_Financial) [November 18, 2026](https://x.com/WOLF_Financial/status/2123016381381714042?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Tariff refunds lifted profit at all three retailers, a one-time help that says little about underlying demand. Energy was the weakest of the eleven sectors, down 3.2%, as crude fell on a larger-than-expected rise in US oil inventories.

**Why it matters:** A broad S&P 500 fund is now about 6% below its October record. Wednesday’s losses were concentrated in health insurers and energy and the gains in retailers and chipmakers outside Nvidia, so what an investor owns mattered more than the index move suggests.

#### QUICK HITS

- **Gold:** Spot gold fell below \$3,800 an ounce for the first time since September 2025 as the dollar strengthened on expectations of higher rates.
- **Housing:** Housing starts rose 9.9% in October from September. Building permits, a sign of future construction, fell 7.4% to their lowest level since May 2020.
- **Inflation abroad:** Consumer prices rose 3.6% from a year earlier in the UK in October, and the euro area’s rate was confirmed at 4.0%, with energy costs driving both.
- **Gas prices:** The national average for regular gas is \$3.75 a gallon, per AAA, down about 19 cents from a week ago.
- **Palo Alto Networks:** The cybersecurity company reported results after the close, raised its forecast for the year and agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for \$4.5 billion in stock.

#### MONEY NOTE

## New I bonds pay 5.51%

Series I savings bonds issued from November 2026 through April 2027 earn a combined rate of **5.51%**, according to TreasuryDirect. That is a fixed rate of 1.40% that lasts for the life of the bond, plus an inflation rate that resets every six months. I bonds cannot be cashed in during the first 12 months, and cashing in before five years gives up the last three months of interest.

- **Thursday:** Anthropic is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq as ANT.
- **Thursday, after the close:** Intuit, Ross Stores and Gap report.
- **Friday, 10:00 a.m. ET:** University of Michigan consumer sentiment, final November reading. Monthly stock options also expire.
- **Monday, Nov 23:** Zoom and Agilent report after the close. Richard McPhail takes over as Home Depot’s CEO.
